Text:
The sternum is three fused bones, which from top to bottom are:

{{c1::manubrium}}

{{c1::body}}

{{c1::xiphoid process}}
Back Extra:
Why: the sternum ossifies from separate pieces that knit together over the years, and the xiphoid process is the last part to ossify.

Cue: the sternum looks like a sword: manubrium = the handle, body = the blade, xiphoid ('sword-shaped') = the tip.

Text: The notch on the top of the manubrium, between the clavicles, is the {{c1::jugular notch}}.
Back Extra: Why: you can feel it as the dip at the base of your neck, right in front of the trachea.

Text: The ridge where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum is the {{c1::sternal angle}}.
Back Extra: Why: the sternal angle is easy to feel and sits level with the second rib, so it is the starting point for counting ribs.

Text: Ribs attach to the sternum by {{c1::costal cartilages}}, which are made of {{c2::hyaline::cartilage type}} cartilage.
Back Extra: Why: flexible cartilage bars let the ribcage spring open each time you breathe instead of acting like a rigid bony box.

Text: The true ribs are ribs {{c1::1–7::rib numbers}}, and each reaches the sternum through {{c2::its own::its own or a shared}} costal cartilage.
Back Extra: Why: 'true' means the rib reaches the sternum on its own; the lower ribs either borrow a neighbor's cartilage or never arrive.

Text: In the BIOL 214 lab's scheme, the false ribs are ribs {{c1::8–12::rib numbers}}; ribs 8–10 reach the sternum only by joining the costal cartilage of rib {{c2::7::rib number}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a false rib has no costal cartilage of its own running to the sternum; ribs 11–12 never reach the sternum at all.

Distinguish: BIOL 313 and the lab manual split them three ways (false = 8–10 only); the BIOL 214 lab counts the floating ribs among the false ribs.

Text: The floating ribs are ribs {{c1::11–12::rib numbers}}, the only ribs with no connection at all to the sternum.
Back Extra: Why: the front ends of ribs 11–12 stop short in the muscles of the abdominal wall; they connect only to the vertebrae behind, so they seem to float.

Back Extra: Why: seven true ribs on each side (ribs 1–7), and 7 × 2 = 14.

Back Extra: Why: one pair of ribs for each of the 12 thoracic vertebrae (12 × 2 = 24).
